articular connections among these components. Existing neural rendering methods 
can predict static 3D object geometries but fall short when dealing with the 
complexity of articulated structures. To address this limitation, we propose a 
pre-processing step that generates a simplified, canonical representation of the 
avatar, enabling efficient processing and improvement of its 3D features through 
a dual encoder technique. Furthermore, we develop a dual encoder image renderer 
capable of handling articulation by conditioning it on the canonical representation 
and integrating a latent articular factor to predict articulation-specific 
geometries. Our approach demonstrates superior quality and efficiency on a large 
dataset of rendered avatars with diverse skin tones, backgrounds, and 
artifications.

Deep learning-based techniques have excelled in image manipulation tasks, but the impact of extreme image modifications on their performance and that of humans remains poorly understood. In this work, we investigate the effects of severe image transformations on classification tasks and human labeling, using a unique dataset with intense, high-frequency changes rendering previous methods ineffectual in reversal. Our research reveals that humans are more tolerant than deep networks of extreme image distortions, but still shares a similar response with machine performance when the image modifications are minimal. These findings highlight the need for further insights from human labeling to enhance the development of robust image manipulation techniques.

The connection between the Askey-Wilson algebra and U$_2$ tangle theories, specifically three-string braid groups within a sphere and the related link symbols, is examined in this study. Leveraging the Lie algebra representation of the three-string braid group, a definite U$_2$ action on the Askey-Wilson algebra is obtained. This action confirms that key generators of the AW algebra can be represented as polynomial invariants of flat U$_2$ connections over a closed surface, demonstrating a U$_2$ connection's link symbol property.

A new set of quantum spin-trimer materials has drawn attention for its unique fractionalized ground states and unusual properties when thin layers are formed, but thorough studies on these materials are still in their early stages. This research focuses on conducting cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a two-dimensional, weakly-coupled spin-trimer model placed on a square lattice, using different computational methods to accurately understand the effect of interlayer coupling. Our results show that as the interlayer coupling becomes stronger, they tend to transform into a well-known spin-1/2 Heisenberg model. We have discovered new two-dimensional ground states that are stable, specifically the vBZ2 state, which is comparable to a famous 2D clock model. Additionally, we found evidence that supports the existence of four distinct domains in the so-called 'quadrupole phase' previously predicted by theoretical models.

Pre-trained language models can perform tasks in multiple areas without direct training, yet their capabilities are not fully utilized due to suboptimal processing of provided hints. To overcome this limitation, we suggest fine-tuning pre-trained models by utilizing a collection of dataset examples and hint examples, then evaluating them on a zero-shot learning framework. Our approach is tested by utilizing a dataset consisting of 20 vision tasks and four hint types, resulting in an overall enhancement of task accuracy from 70.96% to 82.32%. The proposed method can be applied to various other dataset collections, ultimately leading to better understanding and improvement of pre-trained models' behavior.

In extension of the NMSSM with $Z_3$ symmetry, our analysis centers around the
theoretical models where all the singlet doublet components are degenerate.
This degeneracy makes the lightest neutral state a mixture of standard model Higgs and a $R$-parity preserving neutral Higgs bosons as $Z_3$ is broken.
Our analysis focuses on the Nelson-Barr model which has a high predictive power due to the $Z_3$ symmetry and is applied to the electroweak phase shift on the gravitational wave frequency band.
This is done by examining two cases: one with a pure two doublets model where both $A$-fields are aligned in the field space and in another with degenerate two doublets and an isolated singlet $s$.
This is a characteristic of the composite Higgs theory.
Our analysis reveals that in the composite Higgs like scenarios with a pseudo Nambu-Goldstone Higgs and singlet $s$ having a significant coupling mass interaction, the electroweak phase shift on the gravitational wave frequency band can be very significant.
This is done by computing Nelson-Barr model parameters from the dark matter pair annihilation into two lightest neutral states $s$ and the results are given for the graviational wave frequency band and in the graviational wave projects such as DECIGO and LISA.

Designating a single redshift for multiple (sub)millimeter continuum sources within a given high-z field is challenging due to possible differences in source redshifts and lack of precise redshift data. As (sub)millimeter observations become more precise, identifying the exact redshift of each source is crucial for calculating dust emission, radiative transfer, and cosmic chemistry parameters. To address this issue, we developed a tool, high-z Sudoku, to systematically analyze (sub)millimeter and optical/UV spectra to identify robust redshift constraints for each source. This paper outlines the instrument and its initial application to the representative weak-lensings robust redshift reference field South Goochegas and the unproven redshift reference field SXDF-AzTEC1.

To investigate the dynamics of quantum materials in the presence of light, we conducted inelastic neutron scattering on NaYCo2 and studied the results in relation to their structural transformations. The typical antiferromagnetic order in these compounds is destroyed by increasing temperature above a certain point, resulting in a phase with enhanced coherence and a dispersion that shifts to higher energy levels. Additionally, a new liquid phase with specific characteristics emerges from x-ray diffraction experiments, characterized by a certain energy threshold. Our neutron scattering findings support both the liquid and conventional symmetry-breaking descriptions of this transition, suggesting a complex spatial structure in the latter case with distinct components. The data also indicate that certain mechanisms, such as a specific type of magnetic interaction or a bias in the crystal structure, are not required to explain the results, implying that this transition could be a broad phenomenon affecting materials with specific properties, such as those in the family A-site ion-based perovskites.

We've studied how a $SU(3)-$Higgs theory changes from a confined to a deconfined state when we adjust a control parameter, such as the Higgs potential's depth (equivalent to the $t$ parameter in the Standard Model), using a specific method that tests the algorithm's performance over time in different regions. The method involves monitoring two key observables: the average polyopoly configuration and the magnetic energy density. By doing so, we mapped the transition region between these two states and found that it corresponds to a brief, ambiguous phase when the algorithm gets stuck in local energy minima that are neither completely confined nor deconfined. This complex behavior supports our understanding that the algorithm mirrors the model's dynamics in a simple way.

Cr$_2$Al exhibits a significant phase change at 1085 K into a bcc structure, after which it becomes a gas-tight antiferromagnet below 342 K with the antiparallel arrangement of in-plane spin at the body center. Using simulated magnetostructural calculations, the spin arrangement in Cr$_2$Al is validated and the least energetic spin arrangements identified. Notably, the 3D magnetic arrangement in Cr$_2$Al with a Herringbone type is derived from the in-plane spin arrangement with a metastable non-3D antiferromagnetic structure formed through coordination with aluminum's charge. This results in a predictive model outlining how aluminum's position affects magnetic arrangement, exchange interactions, and magnetic behavior. Furthermore, the study highlights that magnetic structure, exchange interactions, and magnetic behavior in certain compounds can also be influenced by the elements they comprise.

A new kinetic model, built upon the extension of the model proposed by Srinivasan, Varvaresou, Burt, and Torrez in [J. Comp. Phys. 223, 63 (2011)], is developed to incorporate the effects of speed-dependent collision frequencies and non-characteristic scattering processes in low-pressure flows. This kinetic model forms a consistent system of gas flow equations, specifically designed for rarefied gases, which can be regimes where the forces of attraction or repulsion between molecules become significant. Crucially, the model is shown to be in perfect agreement with the Boltzmann equation when a correct potential interaction between molecules is applied. In addition to confirming general principles, such as the law of conservation of mass, the model's application to steady flow also yields correct outcomes for entropy and internal energy. Furthermore, as demonstrated with numerical simulations for flow past a cylinder in a vacuum, the model produces accurate predictions of pressure and shearing stress as well as a realistic distribution of velocity. In order to simplify computation, the model is converted into a system of fluid dynamics with variable properties, which has been found to simulate all significant effects of molecule interactions in vacuum environments with molecules that exhibit isotropic behavior when attracting or repelling each other.

To incorporate semantic meaning into game characters by leveraging their understanding of language, we developed Kaji, a compact neural model that translates verbal instructions into actionable commands. Our character system delivers near-human performance in processing semantic directives within interactive stories. Kaji surpasses traditional unconditional baselines and comparable models in achieving more natural and efficient behavior, all achievable with just a minimal amount of training data. We showcase the effectiveness of Kaji in guiding characters within the contexts of a cooking simulation game and a medieval adventure game.

The Electron-Ion Collider's future will involve utilizing electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions to thoroughly investigate the fundamental components of matter. A cutting-edge detector system, incorporating a sophisticated silicon tracker, is being designed for the EIC. This system will precisely pinpoint the position, momentum, identity, and energy of particles produced in collisions, enabling scientists to analyze the internal structure of nucleons and their relationships with gluons. A detailed description of the EIC and its detector will be presented, with a particular focus on the capabilities and characteristics of the silicon tracker, whose development is actively being investigated.

We've observed significant and unusual variations in X-ray light from the active galactic nucleus (AGN) in the Hickson 62 system. These fluctuations in X-ray emission can be seen over a relatively short period of time (less than 300 seconds) multiple times. Previous studies of higher-mass AGNs have revealed similar patterns, thought to be either the effects of energetic plasma or the AGN itself oscillating. The frequency of these fluctuations in X-ray emission in Hickson 62 is remarkably high, averaging around 0.06 millihertz (mHz). The time it takes for the AGN to complete one cycle of oscillation is about 16.9 days. There's also evidence to support a second set of lighter cycles with a frequency of around 0.083 mHz, suggesting a possible period of repetition of this phenomenon. If the observed changes in X-ray emission in Hickson 62 are the result of oscillations, then they appear to be one of the shortest and most frequent occurrences known so far. They also appear to be consistent with the idea that they are driven by the movement of accreting material within the AGN itself. However, in the case of an outburst, it would normally be expected for the AGN to gradually return to its normal state over a period of time. However, during an observation of M81, a distinct low-level fluctuation in X-ray emission with a frequency of around 0.06 mHz was

The study of HD58260, a B-type star with a weak magnetic field, involved using advanced spectropolarimetry to measure its magnetic field characteristics. This technique enables the detection of magnetic field changes within the star's atmosphere through precise polarimetric measurements of specific spectral lines, particularly those with non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects. Spectrograms of HD58260, obtained at the 2.5-meter telescope at the Cassegrain focus, revealed a significant variation in its radial magnetic field, ranging from -34.5 to 5.5 Gauss over two spectral scans, approximately 70 minutes apart. This intense magnetic field fluctuation and the discovered negative field value indicate that HD58260 is a rapidly oscillating magnetic field variable, categorizing it as a MR star according to the Pulsator classification.

A formal connection, referred to as a Dunkl intertwining operator, exists between the space of polynomials with $C_\k$ symmetry and the space of $C_\k$-fold differential operators on the real line, for any finite value of $\k$. A formal representation of this operator in terms of standard basis vectors and the associated shift operator is established, providing an alternative representation to the classical result. This alternative representation is itself a combination of the classical result and an explicit formula that represents the Dunkl intertwining operator as a linear combination of the regular shift operator and a singular operator involving a derivative.

A detailed study of the low-metallicity, starburst galaxy NGC 5253 is being carried out using ALMA compact array observations of the 30 GHz H30α line emission. This study has revealed two main star-forming regions, one of which is confirmed to be extremely dense with a calculated gas temperature of around 40 K. However, another region, dubbed "Region C", has a seemingly normal density and an estimated gas temperature of approximately 12 K. Following further analysis using line-ratio methods, it was determined that both regions exhibit high levels of star-formation efficiency, equivalent to 50-60%, a characteristic also found in the Crab Nebula and the Merger galaxy NGC 6090. Using the star-forming rate formula developed by Karim et al., it was discovered that the starburst activity in both regions began around 10 million years ago and is set to continue for the next 0.7 million years. Furthermore, it was calculated that the gas in both regions has a high metal content of around 0.01 solar values. This study has significant implications; it suggests that the initial metal content required to initiate a highly efficient starburst is much lower than initially thought, requiring only one thousandth of the solar value. Additionally, it appears that the initial metal content necessary for the formation of massive star-forming regions is much less than that necessary for the formation of compact, dense regions.

This note demonstrates that if a continuous orbit map from a $1$-dimensional solenoid has a rigid boundary under the condition that its induced map on the solenoid is conjugate to a hyperbolic matrix, then this orbit map is topologically inflexible. Moreover, we establish a sufficient criterion for the solenoid to produce maps that meet this inflexibility condition. Consequently, we derive a condition under which continuous $G$-orbits in $3$-dimensional space, where $G$ is a virtually cyclic group, are topologically inflexible.

This study presents an in-depth examination of the strong uniform convergence of various nonparametric estimators for which there is a high level of prior knowledge available. Convergence is established for specific types of set-valued functions, including those with random boundaries and those containing random elements. Real-world applications, particularly in the fields of econometrics and statistical medicine, feature conditional expectation functions with these characteristics, as do existing theories and methods, often assuming strong prior knowledge. To our knowledge, this analysis represents the first comprehensive study of the strong convergence of kernel estimators for multivariate conditional value-at-risk functions, which involve lower semi-variability bounds and represent a particularly challenging case.

To track the unfolding dynamics of an epidemic within a city, a non-intrusive state estimation framework is crucial for decision-making. The proposed Observer framework consists of a state model, designed to predict epidemic development, and a dynamic observer that generates accurate representations of the true state. The effectiveness of this approach relies on the established non-linear relationships between key variables. The effectiveness of the Observer framework was demonstrated through computer simulations modeling different types of epidemics.

Link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs has significant utility for both extrapolation and prediction, offering valuable insights that can be used to complete missing knowledge graph components and generate hypothetical scenarios. Current methods primarily focus on static features, neglecting the temporal characteristics of these graphs, which are crucial for accurately predicting future relationships. To address this oversight, this study introduces a novel link forecasting approach centered on a static framework that leverages temporal features to forecast upcoming connections in a knowledge graph. The proposed approach involves developing a static model and employing different temporal features to optimize prediction outcomes. The model's effectiveness was evaluated across multiple benchmarks, with results indicating a notable improvement in forecasting accuracy.

Research on ultrashshort pulse generation in high-power ultrashshort pulse lasers has made significant progress with recent studies, but investigations into their operation are still incomplete. This study contributes to the expansion of this field by conducting an in-depth analysis of an anti-resonance, high-power ring laser. Utilizing a combination of theoretical (stab-analysis) and numerical (simulations) methods, this research explores the stable pulse operation and frequency-soliton states of the laser. Notably, the research discovered novel stable modes of operation, including spiral frequency-soliton states, which occur at lower pump levels than previously thought possible. These unusual properties are attributed to the distinct properties of high-power anti-resonance cobalt lasers.

A growing trend in machine learning research, federated learning seeks to develop robust, data-hungry models using distributed client devices. Yet, a major challenge in this area is the significant variation in training resources, such as processing speed, memory, and energy efficiency, which severely hampers performance when models are combined. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel asynchronous collaborative learning method to train nonlinear regression models efficiently, considering each device has limited computing capacity and energy lifespan. Our approach, CAFENO, features three key components: a resource-aware model selection process, a strategy to manage model diversity, and a strategy for nonlinear regression tasks. Through our simulations, we demonstrate that CAFENO outperforms leading competitors, such as MOFANA and PerFM, by achieving better accuracy, reduced computation costs, and extended energy durability.

The efficiency of solar cells can be enhanced by using thin silicon layers. In such direct silicon layers, the back wall is absent, which results in the loss of a valuable conversion factor. To prevent loss of light, a technique called Bragg screening is employed. A Bragg screening model, which is a 3D structure, has been shown to prevent reflection from the rear interface. In a study, a rear Bragg screen with a spatial structure was analyzed to examine its effect on a thin silicon solar cell's light absorption properties. Various simulations were conducted to identify the optimal device parameters, which showed that a Bragg screen with an average hole size of 2 $\mu$m supported six orders of frequency and achieved a maximum absorption rate of 99.5% in a 50 $\mu$m silicon layer. Additionally, the study found that a 1 $\mu$m thick silicon layer could achieve absorption consistent with a much thicker layer, specifically 820 $\mu$m, without the Bragg screen, while still meeting the requirement for high energy absorption.

We take a holistic approach to solving one particular branch of the solution to the equation $y = e^{e^{y-1}}$.  One-Eighth strategy will be used to develop a method of solving this equation that can be extended to solving other branches of the solution to the equation.  This new technique generates a distinct set of solutions for $y$ in terms of $\lambda$, where these expressions are in the form of power series.  We learn that when a particular condition is met - when $\lambda$ is greater than $0.4321257$ - these expressions become invalid.  In addition, we learn that another set of power series, this time satisfying a different condition related to $\lambda$, is in fact the correct solution to the equation.  Ultimately, in order to better understand how this particular piece of work contributes to the study of tetration, we take a step back in time and revisit the initial formulation of the problem.  In doing so, we learn that an infinite number of distinct solutions for the equation will be generated, one for each iteration of the hexagon approach, and we learn which of these distinct solutions will ultimately work.  In the process, we study not only tetration but also certain concepts surrounding the tetration and solve various problems related to it, where one problem in particular involves determining when a particular expression is correct across all real valued $\lambda$; this particular problem leads to the establishment of certain distinct criteria or tests.

We propose a novel construction of high-dimensional expander graphs with various properties. These graphs meet specific criteria related to their dimension, girth, and edge counts while also satisfying a particular condition related to their covering radius. The examples generated by our method include (infinitely many) infinite dimensional expander graphs, which have the potential to be used as topologies in physics and other fields. The class of these infinite dimensional expanders is particularly significant because their girth approaches infinity, meeting a condition required in certain theoretical studies of complex systems. Additionally, our method allows for the creation of sparse high-dimensional expanders that outperform existing alternatives in terms of edge count. Lastly, we've demonstrated that our method produces graphs that not only have the desired high-dimensional expansion property but also hold an important condition in graph theory, specifically non-amalgamability.

Researchers investigated the magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb crystal GdInO3 through direct current susceptibility measurements and a detailed analysis of its zero-field cooled magnetization. Their findings revealed a temperature-dependent magnetization curve that could be interpreted using an effective spin-7/2 model in the presence of interactions that couple spin components. The results also indicated the presence of short-range exchange interactions that cause a collective spin state at the temperature transition. Furthermore, the data demonstrated that GdInO3 exhibits a 2D behavior at temperatures below 1.8K.

Predicting missing connections in networks, or link forecasting, has significant implications for understanding disease transmission and molecular interactions.
We introduced a novel, efficient neural network approach called SSNE for making link predictions in large, sparse networks.
By using an early stop strategy in training, SSNE significantly reduces memory and time requirements.
We tested SSNE on various real-world datasets and found it outperformed other methods using predictive measures.
The implementation of SSNE's core algorithm can be accessed on our dedicated GitHub repository.

A novel silicon atomic vapor chamber, incorporating a 10 cm deepablation zone within an ultra-low-stress silicon membrane, has been successfully miniaturized to fit a 1 cm by 0.4 cm width area, as demonstrated by electron microscopy images. This structure features a 10 nanometer thick layer of native oxide, reducing heat capacity in the membrane. Using a 12 watt laser power supply, a 1 millimeter by 0.4 mm region at the top membrane can be heated to 1958 Kelvin, while maintaining a 10 millimeter long by 1 millimeter wide atomic vapor column. This design enables individual atom manipulation, allowing for independent control over individual atoms. This new design sets a new standard for the smallest atomic vapor chambers, surpassing previous 1.8 cubic centimeter designs, and introducing a new capability for integrated circuit-based vapor chambers.

We create mathematical representations of nonlinear distortion for two types of complex signal formats: dual-polarization QAM 4D formats with varied phase differences and dual-polarization PAM-4 formats. Our analysis combines the Fourier Bochner method with the second moment approach from [1] to gauge the impact of various factors like crosstalk, coupling, and differential phase shift on nonlinear distortion in each format. Our findings are then verified through practical experiments.

Large, complex datasets are typically inaccessible in real-time through conventional analysis methods, necessitating the creation of a new approach for rapid wildfire monitoring. A novel deep learning technique has been developed called FIRe-GAN, a fusion method that integrates near-infrared and visible wildfire images for enhanced detail and texturing. FIRe-GAN employs a multi-stage process involving a pixel-level fusion algorithm and a generator from the U-net framework, facilitated by a side-to-side fusion approach. The output is optimized through a patch-to-image loss and a gradient loss in the style of FIRe-GAN's original loss function. The technique allows for real-time wildfire visualization in both lab and real-world settings. A comprehensive evaluation of FIRe-GAN is presented, including a comparison with standard fusion techniques and an assessment of its performance on actual wildfire images.

Despite substantial research on detecting depression from social media texts, 
unresolved questions remain regarding the depression label's validity and the impact of data preprocessing on performance. 
Most existing studies relied on crowdsourced annotations rather than clinically verified depression diagnoses.

We gathered a unique social media dataset annotated by both crowdsource and clinical evaluators, 
and compared the outcomes of using annotated texts directly with those resulting from pre-processing techniques commonly used in previous studies.

Our results show that pre-processing methods can alter the composition of training and testing data, 
leading to inconsistent performances across pre-processing techniques and data labels.

We also found that data preprocessing can shift the distribution of depression symptoms in training data, 
resulting in poor generalization to unseen data and real depression cases.

Therefore, we recommend using clinically validated annotations and data preprocessing methods that preserve original text meanings rather than truncating them. 

Our SocialMediaDep dataset, comprising social media posts from patients with depression and a crowdsource-controlled method for distributing raw texts during training, is made available for future research on depression detection and related topics.

We introduce a novel stochastic model for COVID-19 that mirrors a particular probabilistic process. This model is based on a traditional SIR model, incorporating symptoms and severe cases, with the assumption that susceptible and recovered populations remain stable, while infected individuals evolve according to a first-order Markov process defined by the basic pandemic process's generating function. By characterizing this function, we derive expressions for the expected number of severe cases and the probability distribution of total infections. Furthermore, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the model's components as the pandemic process becomes infinitely complex.

The ISGMR and a $3^- $ state coupled with an ISQMR excitation in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si nuclei were studied through inelastic scattering with an $^{16}$O beam and charged-particle techniques. By analyzing the cross sections, we derived the strength distributions and calculated the energy-weighted sums of the ISGMR and a $3^- $ state coupled with an ISQMR. We evaluated the impact of coupling between the ISGMR and a $3^- $ state using two methods: the coupled-cluster with a perturbative correction method and the static quadrupole correlation operator method. Results showed that the latter method provided a good description of the observed strength distributions and the energy shifts of the ISGMR coupled with a $3^- $ state. We concluded that the ISGMR and a $3^- $ state coupled with an ISQMR exhibit distinct characteristics and that the former can be accurately described by a single-particle or collective excitation. However, a $3^- $ is directly coupled with an ISQMR and displays a unique two-branch structure resulting from a coupling with an ISQMR. This work also highlights the importance of a $3^- $ in $^{24}$Mg and provides a criterion for measuring the characteristic time of an ISQMR.

Systems featuring stick-slip behavior, governed by the principles of friction, appear at various scales - from human body movements to geophysical tectonic plate movements. The stick-slip phenomenon occurs when a dynamic system with rapid motion is hindered by a opposing force, with its behavior ultimately driven by the force of friction that stalls its progress. Theoretical models of this phenomenon often center around simplified representations of a static frictional barrier, with its impeding force being represented as a threshold that must be exceeded by the dynamic system's momentum. The resulting models, which include elements of both spring and frictional systems, can exhibit stable or unstable patterns of movement, depending on the interplay between their stored energy and resistance to further motion. The study of these models typically focuses on their behavior when the dynamic system is in a state of motion, with the opposing force being a fixed aspect of the model. This work explores the potential for these systems to be modified in response to their motion, with their behavior depending on the rate at which their motion is interrupted. The study examines the characteristics of these regulatory systems, which include both ideal and damped models, with both cases demonstrating comparable behavior. The model used in this study is based on a simple system with mass, spring, and frictional elements, with its behavior governed by a simple equation that adjusts for motion and resistance. The researchers then examine the phases of motion within this system, which include both rapid and sluggish movements, with its behavior governed by different principles

Time series analysis in financial markets often employs powerful, complex models that are difficult to implement, featuring steep learning curves that hinder small to medium-sized businesses from using them. To address this issue, a set of novel, parameterized models is introduced, specifically tailored for time series analysis applications, and generalized dynamic network flows are utilized to provide solutions for these models that are expressible in polynomial time. Surprisingly, it is demonstrated that solving these models often necessitates an in-depth, multi-layered Bellman equation, requiring capabilities that go beyond standard dynamic programming approaches. Nonetheless, a new hedging strategy is developed, proving its superiority over traditional methods on a range of synthetic and real-world market scenarios.

In today's commercial recommender systems, understanding and catering to the hidden motivations of users can significantly enhance their experience and loyalty. Despite its significance, there is a noticeable knowledge gap in this area. This research pioneers the development of an intelligent system that explicitly identifies and fulfills users' underlying purposes. A novel method, referred to as Hidden User Motivation Modeling, is proposed to determine the most probable reason behind a user's current action. By continuously estimating reason probabilities, the system dynamically shifts from one context to another and recommends items accordingly. Experimental results on a vast real-world dataset showcase the effectiveness of this approach, surpassing baseline models in both case reason identification and recommendation performance.

The structure of a particular nonlinear differential equation, known as a general symmetric unfolding of the source, is analyzed and its connection to a specific type of special function is established, revealing that it can be expressed in terms of a transformed version of a particular special function called the double confluent Heun function. This relationship leads to a complete set of solutions to the unfolding, expressed as a series of special functions, for certain initial conditions. The specific form of these solutions, expressed as a series of transformed double confluent Heun functions, is derived algebraically, revealing a pattern in the coefficients, and providing a method to calculate solutions for initial conditions that do not meet certain criteria. The solutions are shown to be singular, concentrating near certain points, and through a coordinate transformation, the general form of the solutions is obtained, revealing a pattern that provides a method to calculate solutions for initial conditions that do not meet the criteria. The derivation of the equation, a particular special function, and the series of special functions, is established through a formal power series approach, and the singular behavior of the solutions, and the series of special functions, is established, and through a coordinate transformation, the singular behavior of the solutions, and the series of special functions, is established.

The matrix approximation with groupwise heterogeneity transforms a matrix into a low-rank approximation by combining matrix components based on predefined categories. The number of these categories is typically set in advance and we investigate how matrix properties influence this number's determination. Theoretical models, such as the Poisson regression matrix, are too complex for concrete analysis, so we focus on a simpler matrix structure that captures key behaviors from the Poisson model. The number of categories is shown to converge to a specific value, which is influenced by the matrix's characteristics, when the matrix dimensions become infinite. The convergence rate is affected by the matrix's non-cohesive properties and the non-linear transformation applied to its components. The determination of this specific value is achieved by studying a mathematical problem in which a geometric shape's volume is minimized under constraints, resulting in a point formation that encompasses exponentially growing distances. The existence and uniqueness of this formation are proven, as well as the existence of an optimal solution for this geometric problem, providing a mathematical tool that can be applied to matrix approximation as well.

This paper outlines a novel framework of particle physics. To achieve this, we first need to recognize that existing theories are inadequate, particularly when attempting to describe the origin of mass as a distinct physical phenomenon. Next, we will summarize the core elements of our proposed framework, highlighting how the concept of symmetry serves as a key characteristic but is noticeably absent at the starting point. Finally, we will explore significant indicators and suggestions present in the lack of symmetry that pave the way for a new particle physics and the potential connection of our theory to string theory.

We introduce a new observable, $R_{\ell}^S$, to study semi-inclusive processes resulting from the $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition, where $\ell$ can be either muon or electron. The proposed observable is similar to the LFC equality ratio $R_D^S$, but involves a more inclusive approach by considering the hadronic final state more generally, thereby enhancing its sensitivity to the Wilson coefficients of QCD non-relativistic operators involved. Its theoretical expression is provided in terms of the underlying New Physics contributions.

We address the problem of helping multi-channel linear systems maintain their positions near optimal equilibrium points in the presence of external disturbances. A novel information structure for decentralized control systems is introduced, allowing for the design of the so-called decentralized plug-and-play (DPp) method. This approach ensures that even when some sub-systems encounter stochastic disturbances or hardware failures, the global system stays near its desired state, and importantly, no global controller or actuator is needed. A key benefit of the DPp method is that it enables flexible online additions or removals of sub-systems without affecting the performance or stability of the remaining systems. Furthermore, the DPp method allows for the efficient sharing of actuation resources among sub-systems. A distinctive aspect of the DPp method is that it enables the simultaneous handling of information decentralization, actuation sharing, and online reconfigurability. We derive the design of the DPp method under specific assumptions and demonstrate its applicability to a range of practical systems, including large-scale, cross-coupled, and nonlinear systems. A key innovation is that the DPp method preserves the dimension of each individual controller, despite its global design, and thus, it significantly reduces the computational complexity of the design process. A practical application of the DPp method is that it enables the efficient adaptation of robotic team training, where individual robots are used to model, simulate, and train their counterparts in a multi-agent collaborative robot project.

The COVID-19 pandemic has become one of the most severe health crises in recent years, spreading across the globe and claiming millions of lives. As the outbreak gained momentum, the scientific community has come together to develop innovative solutions to combat the disease. This has resulted in an unprecedented number of research papers being published each day to address various aspects of the pandemic. To streamline the processing of this research paper avalanche, a computational method was devised to filter out papers lacking practical applications and assign a reliability score to those with more credible claims. This paper introduces a cutting-edge paper validation method that leverages BERT attributes and a two-stage classifier, trained on a comprehensive dataset gathered from Semanticscholar, to distinguish scientific articles related to COVID-19. The proposed approach achieves a level of accuracy similar to human categorization, as evaluated using two datasets from Twitter and a general corpus.

Network research encompasses a broad spectrum of topics, from basic concepts of graph theory to the intricate analysis of real-world network data. This comprehensive overview aims to provide a detailed atlas of network research terminology, serving as a valuable reference for both novice students and seasoned professionals seeking to enhance their understanding of the subject.

Over the past two decades, extensive research has been conducted on eco-evolutionary dynamics in various contexts. Many studies have used classical epidemiological and evolutionary models, focusing on the interplay between evolution and infectious dynamics that occur on similar timescales. In contrast, this review looks back at early developments in eco-evolutionary theory, where predictions often assumed long-term changes rather than short-term dynamics. We suggest that, from an eco-evolutionary perspective, the significant effects of genetic change can occur rapidly, influenced by factors such as genetic diversity, the generation time, and the rate of disease transmission. We provide a conceptual framework for understanding these factors and their impact on the timescale of evolutionary change. We also review the implications of our findings for the study of infectious dynamics and evolutionary change in real-world systems.

A collaborative approach is proposed to evaluate the effectiveness of speech self-supervised models in withstanding adversarial challenges. By applying a range of hostile modes derived from existing benchmarks to multiple models at various training epochs, our research examines the hostile susceptibility patterns of these models. The results indicate that speech models are more prone to adversarial attacks early in the training process, but also show significantly reduced vulnerability as the models mature, indicating improved robustness. Furthermore, our study reveals that the hostile susceptibility pattern differs depending on the type of speech representation being learned, and we develop a hostile robustness assessment metric based on this finding, providing insight into the hostile adaptation process in speech self-supervised learning.
This study offers an integrative examination of the implications that emerge at the intersection of blockchains and decentralized online marketplaces.

A proposed solution to address concerns about data analysis fairness and privacy is to calculate an E-value, which serves as a rough equivalent to a p-value but takes into account confounding factors, as opposed to adjusting by propensity scores. This approach, however, has a limitation: it assumes all relevant confounding variables are included in the model, a claim that might be flawed. To address this shortcoming, we suggest a method to assess whether the E-value remains a reliable metric when this condition is not met. Our system comprises three main parts: the first involves using a posterior probability assessment to determine the likelihood that all essential confounding variables were part of the model, and if not, whether it is possible to identify additional crucial variables. The second component outlines an iterative process to evaluate the E-value confidence interval and whether it intersects with zero. The third part presents an illustrative case study that demonstrates our proposed framework.

The study of quantum invariant properties in bijective combinatorics is closely
linked to the theory of the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetric Laurent polynomial
series over the rational function field $\mathbb{C}(q)$. We systematically
catalogue the distinct classes of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry that exist
within this type of series. The paper provides a comprehensive outline of the
relevant properties associated with each symmetry class, encompassing any
potential universal characteristics, the specific properties of series equipped
with this symmetry, and examples of invariant functions that fall under this
category. The research demonstrates that the key characteristics of each
$U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry subfamily can be derived from the properties of
the two foundational cases, known as Type I and Type II symmetries. The paper
also presents a detailed classification of the Type I symmetries, which exhibits
a direct analogy to the theory of determinant sequences. Additionally, the
research highlights a set of distinct, non-unital $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetry
cases that are distinct from those involving the power series. We utilize this
newly established classification, alongside a pre-existing theory due to
Garscia-Perera-Ku, to identify and categorize generalized $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$

The Internet of Vehicles is becoming a reality, with implications for our daily lives, thanks to advancements in modern technologies like cloud computing and advanced wireless networks. A key component, vehicle-to-vehicle communication, supports essential functions like collision avoidance systems and navigation, although these data-rich environments make them vulnerable to cyber threats. Machine learning, particularly with its deep learning aspects, has shown potential in thwarting these risks, though it too has security limitations when considering data privacy, especially with sensitive information involved in vehicles' vicinity. A promising approach, Federated Learning, offers promise in mitigating these security issues though its efficiency is another story. A blockchain-based framework for FL can enhance security, security but also raises concerns over computation and communication overhead, especially with blockchain's distributed architecture causing extra costs in terms of time and monetary resources, a challenge to be overcome in IoT vehicles' environment. This review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and pitfalls in achieving secure FL in IoT vehicles and proposes a blockchain-based framework to tackle those challenges and pitfalls.

The beauty and elegance of parton-medium interactions are examined through non-prompt and prompt D meson production in proton-lead collisions at the LHC's highest energy.  Elegance, conveying the idea of beauty or charm in particle physics terms, refers to the presence of these quarks in proton-lead collisions.  A comprehensive theoretical model is used to measure the beauty and elegance production cross-sections at a proton-proton collision energy of 5.02 TeV, based on data from the ALICE detector.  Specifically, distributions of D meson transverse momentum are measured within a specified central rapidity range, and are normalized over a specific charged particle multiplicity range, known as centrality.  A key observation is that beauty and elegance, existing in proton-lead collisions, are remarkably stable across different centralities, suggesting that they are entirely a result of the in-medium interactions between partons and beauty or charm quarks.  Additionally, ratios of non-prompt to prompt D meson production are measured, providing further insight into the production mechanisms of beauty and elegance.  A distinct pattern is observed in these ratios, indicating a significant increase in beauty and elegance, as a result of nuclear collisions.

The long-term aim of Quantum Computing at Very Low Temperatures (QaVLT), a program based at Fermilab, is to leverage vast government funding to develop superconducting quantum processors that utilize vast laser-cooled aluminum lattices at millikelvin temperatures, yielding thousands of high-performance qubits. This initiative is seen as a competitive boost to the current quantum computing efforts at national laboratories, with the potential to produce significant technological advancements at the interface of quantum computing and particle physics. This program is also exploring the creation of specialized platforms for topological quantum computing, spin-based quantum computing, and hybrid platforms that integrate different quantum systems, all situated within highly shielded and superconducting cleanrooms. We recommend using the Research and Development (R&D) funding to develop and construct cutting-edge, laboratory-sized teststands that incorporate state-of-the-art cryogenic and micromachining techniques, tailored to support the unique research objectives of each targeted quantum computing architecture. These specialized teststands will maintain exceptionally strong magnetic fields, achieved through the use of cryogenic magnetometers with significant financial support. This program is also proposing the development of a highly innovative "quantum cooler" device set to break ground at the Fermilab site in 2023, offering a user-friendly interface between dilution refrigerators and helium-3 superfluid layers that could revolutionize future large-scale quantum computing at very low temperatures.

Many developers and security professionals are aware of the vulnerabilities of cryptographic functions, however, incorrect implementations can compromise entire systems. Existing studies mainly focus on publicly visible code, such as public repositories on GitHub, which might not reflect the entire landscape of cryptographic implementations across the entire web. Our research targets a more significant goal, aiming to identify and analyze real-world projects, whether they're open-source or not, to gain a more comprehensive understanding of cryptographic best practices. Our tool, PyACT, has successfully scanned 1.8 million Python projects on GitHub, pinpointing potential security risks and providing guidance for remediation. Our findings not only validate known vulnerabilities but also uncover novel ones, serving as a warning to the Python community. Moreover, we'll make our data available to study cryptographic practices in other programming languages.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in urban remote sensing and mapping fields, with the integration of deep learning leveraging large-scale, open-source, and annotated dataset contributions. However, the cost of manual annotation for urban environment objects such as buildings and roads becomes economically unfeasible for broad datasets and applications. This paper presents an innovative framework, VALUE, which utilizes user engagement and social influence to obtain high-quality label assignments for selected objects in urban environments with the aid of crowdsourcing. For prioritization, we employ a network-based approach to determine influential users and their potential for label contribution. The VALUE framework then applies a voting system with both intra-user and inter-user processes in place to refine label candidates. The performance of VALUE is demonstrated through its successful labeling of a 500k image dataset, split across three cities globally, yielding impressive results for urban scene object detection and segmentation tasks.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework, the NuSPAN Network, specifically tailored for addressing the challenges of the seismic inversion problem through deep learning. The issue of incomplete and limited data with significant noise in seismic recordings poses substantial obstacles to reconstructing the internal structure of the subsurface earth arrangement. The presented NuSPAN Network incorporates a sophisticated layer that can interpret the spatially varying properties of the earth's arrangement, with a regularization technique that prevents overfitting by introducing a penalty for nonuniform sparse distributions. The framework's ability to separately process amplitude and non-amplitude information is another key innovation, which significantly enhances the accuracy and flexibility of the reconstruction. The performance of the NuSPAN Network is thoroughly evaluated by conducting comprehensive numerical experiments designed to test its ability to handle diverse scenarios, such as nonuniform earth properties, irregular seismic data acquisition, and simulated seismic inverse problems at various levels of difficulty. The results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed framework in achieving exceptional reconstruction accuracy and robustness, with the potential to be applied in various mathematical and nonmathematical inverse problems.

The paper explores several linear semigroups of operators derived from the composition with a free analytic function. It considers specific types of function norms, including BMOA, BMOA$_0$, VMOA, and BLOA norms, and obtains the sufficiency of certain conditions for weak continuity, in addition to finding semigroup type conditions that guarantee norm continuity. Moreover, the paper investigates the equivalence between the weak and strong types of these semigroups. It also discusses the alpha-limits of the geometric means of these semigroups, establishes the closedness of the BMOA, BMOA$_0$, VMOA, and BLOA norms under these semigroups, and analyzes the essentiality and zero properties of the range and kernel of these semigroups. Finally, the paper establishes several equivalent characterizations for the BMOA, BMOA$_0$, VMOA, and BLOA norms as well as for the BLOA norm's weak and strong types of semigroups.

Study of entanglement properties in compact systems indicates that a particular form of entanglement between neighboring parts is a fundamental property, present across various systems. It's necessary to distinguish this property, which the research calls 'operator merging,' from another measure, quantum entanglement. To understand operator merging, we analyze it through wavefunction overlaps, developing a method to calculate it by determining the dimension of the space that contains the combined states. We show that this method works by calculating the way eigenstates of adjacent parts change relative to one another within the total space, and we find that operator merging typically exhibits distinct behavior on both small and very large scales. We find that a particular type of model, which we call the Haagerup model, does not exhibit this behavior, and instead, as the total number of parts grows without bounds, the merging of operators stops being universal. We conclude this universal behavior only occurs in systems with a finite number of parts.

Accurate part-of-speech annotation is a foundational element for understanding language patterns and relationships across time periods. While annotations from past projects can be leveraged for current research, the accuracy issues common in historical language corpora pose a significant problem, leading to numerous errors and inaccuracies. Existing corrections methods primarily rely on current-language part-of-speech models, which are ineffective when dealing with historical language variants. We propose a novel, context-based approach for part-of-speech identification that considers previous researcher's labels as informative cues. This method views the annotation process as a joint optimization problem and applies an integer programming algorithm to derive a set-valued prediction that aims to maximize the likelihood of accurate labels and their combinations. Experimentally, our approach demonstrates a 25.7% enhancement in corpus accuracy over standard correction methods, while also successfully handling under-defined and ambiguous cases.

We've developed a new approach to evaluating the convergence of a specific type of mathematical series. This framework is particularly useful for analyzing power series. By comparing the rates at which the terms of a power series converge, we establish a criterion for the series that enables us to find its radius and even extend its expansion to points outside the original interval of convergence. This theory has been thoroughly explored, with numerous theorems and examples demonstrating its applications. We've also introduced innovative methods for applying a specific type of mathematical transformation to a power series, which allows us to gain a deeper understanding of its properties. This has been achieved through the development of two types of convergent mappings that enable us to analyze the behavior of a power series in different ways, with a specific type of mathematical convergence called $\beta$-convergence playing a crucial role in this process. By developing this concept, we've been able to establish the existence of special types of mathematical fields that enable us to extend the expansion of a power series. This has been achieved through the development of two types of mathematical fields that play a crucial role in this process. Furthermore, we've been able to derive a set of criteria that enable us to analyze the behavior of a specific type of mathematical series called a m-series. This has been achieved through the development of a new approach to mathematical series that involves applying mathematical transformations to determine their convergence properties. Cities are increasingly leveraging Information and Communication Technologies, like Smart Cities, to enhance residents' quality of life and efficiency in management. As part of these efforts, cities develop various services such as public transportation systems, traffic control, and construction supervision, necessitating a broad range of software applications. To address these needs, cities often provide non-technical users with requirements, which must be translated into a machine-readable format to implement. This process can be time-consuming and labor-intensive if requirements are ill-defined or inconsistent, posing a risk of incorrect implementation. Furthermore, existing solutions either lack semantical support or are fully automated, failing to accommodate non-technical users' varying levels of detail. This paper proposes an assistant tool that helps cities meet these challenges by formalizing specifications and offers a middle ground between full automation and manual processing. The tool not only provides a formal specification but also highlights essential elements missing from the requirements. These key features are derived from the city's organizational knowledge, such as policies and best practices. To facilitate understanding, the tool's interface includes visual aids like an overview of cities' organizational knowledge, as well as a comparison of formal specifications with the initial requirements, highlighting differences and similarities. A case study demonstrates the tool's capabilities by transforming a city's public transportation requirements into a formal specification. This software is available in open-source, open-access, and through public-private partnership models.

To utilize superconducting quantum processors efficiently, reliable data storage and processing with high fidelity error rates is essential. Despite current progress, physical errors in operations remain a significant constraint. This study explores quantum error correction (QEC) through the application of the concealed inverses protocol on a specific superconducting quantum architecture. The process, involving the insertion of inverse gates to neutralize operational errors, was examined in the context of non-uniform magnetic flux-driven quantum devices that exhibit naturally suppressed $ZZ$ gate correlations. Simulations revealed that the majority of errors can be remedied with a relatively small number of concealed inverse gates. This research offers an alternative approach to existing quantum error correction methods and provides a specific example of a robust superconducting quantum architecture that can execute the concealed inverses protocol efficiently.

In a category that satisfies regularity, like topological categories, subobjects can be represented as binary depictions (like groups of subobjects meeting at a point). However, in categories where the regular and exisential closures intersect (like certain non-topological categories), such depictions do not exist. In a different context, for a preorder to be depictured as a subobject, it needs to be represented by a family of subobjects that have a common upper bound. In a case where a preorder's representation by such a family is equivalent to the preorder being complete, the depiction is considered valid. In a category where the exisential and regular closures intersect, such depictions are known as cocartesian. This study aims to understand how these cocartesian depictions work in a category. It is shown that in a case where a category's exisential and regular closures intersect, a preorder's family of subobjects that have an upper bound will result in a valid depiction if and only if the family is connected. A connection is also established between the equational properties of a category and the topology of a category's depictions. In a case where a category's exisential and regular closures are the same, a non-abelian category's depictions are shown to have a certain structure that is similar to the depictions found in categories with distributive lattices.

To characterize the spatial variability of marine extremes, we propose a multivariate statistical model for monitoring and understanding extreme events with temporal dependencies and patterns of correlation. The model defines a level of severity based on the intensity of associated events and identifies a "peaks over thresholds" framework to weigh the likelihood of concurrent extreme events. The likelihood of such events is measured by the probability of two or more variables exceeding their threshold in a specified area. The model incorporates temporal correlations and spatial correlations in a Bayesian analysis of data, adjusted for potential systematic errors in data collection. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulation and a real-world application examining environmental patterns in sea temperature and pressure around New Zealand.

Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn general visual data. Nevertheless, its performance is limited by visual confusions and linguistic ambiguities. To effectively derive meaningful semantics from images and text combinations, it is crucial for a model to be able to accurately interpret the complex interplay between images and text. To address this challenge, we present a straightforward yet effective approach that enhances the accuracy of visual-textual matching for CLIP models. This technique involves utilizing multiple forms of supplementary text inputs, which are specifically designed to aid in visual learning and comprise diverse linguistic patterns and visual cues. By incorporating these assisting text variants, it is possible to learn semantic concepts of different visual categories, thereby broadening the scope of visual understanding. As a result, it can be observed that our approach enhances the accuracy of state-of-the-art CLIP models across various applications, such as image-classification and visual retrieval tasks.

The concept of noisy maps has been applied to the process of reversing the effects of a noisy transformation on an arbitrary vector. In a preceding study, the requirements for a linear transformation to be invertible and the cost function of the inverse process were specified, with the determination of the inverse map (noise cancellation method) being proven to be universally optimal. This study expands on that work by relaxing the conditions on the linear transformation, allowing it to be represented by an arbitrary matrix, with the effect of noise still being accurately accounted for under a broader definition of invertibility.

We explicitly identify and categorize the segments of quaternionic spectral categories, which are akin to Eilenberg-Mac Lane categories for certain types of quaternionic spectra. The work builds on previous research into braided and unitary spectral categories, incorporating concepts from Clifford algebras and referring to relevant literature for a thorough understanding. The approach involves a combination of mathematical invariants based on various properties, such as the Lane-Bloch spectrum, total dimension, and fermion condensation. Furthermore, we establish connections between these invariants and categories related to Clifford algebras, as well as a spectral category that is analogous to the Eilenberg-Mac Lane category for integer coefficients. The research culminates in a comprehensive classification of quaternionic spectral categories, which is presented in a geometric fashion.

Let's consider a Noetherian local ring R with a certain parameter x and an ideal I generated by x, along with a task of determining when the ring R/I satisfies specific conditions related to an invariant property F. This task is a natural extension of earlier research that analyzed the properties of rings in terms of Hilbert functions. Now, the goal is to capitalize on the simplicity of Hilbert functions to establish criteria for rings in relation to the Frobenius map. This new task allows us to provide upper bounds on the highest possible Hilbert functions for rings of a specific type, which in turn yields consequences for rings with certain characteristics, such as reduced Krull dimension and those that are tightly closed in a larger structure.

In pathology and radiology, deep learning models are increasingly being employed to deliver patient-specific diagnostic information, yet their outputs are often presented in the DICOM standard despite not originally being generated within this format. This paper introduces a Python framework called Highdicom, which is designed to standardize and simplify the processing of image-based data by integrating the DICOM standard. With Highdicom, users can convert model data into DICOM format or alternatively read in DICOM files and convert the information into a more accessible Python format, facilitating further analysis. Furthermore, Highdicom includes a module for natural language processing that can enhance the quality of image annotations or translate the outputs of models without DICOM expertise into a more understandable format. This software is released under a free and open license to support the seamless integration of deep learning and traditional image annotation and reporting workflows.

We show that the surface charge of Einstein-Hilbert action is zero under conditions of constant curvature and varying dimensions.  In a case of changing curvature in holographic setup, this implies the monodromy matrix elements of disformally related systems are identity matrices.  We find that Lagrangian form of surface term, along with a related Noether current, vanish in a specific scenario of changing curvature coupled with Weyl scaling.  In a case of constant curvature in AdS spacetime, this surface term is finite and purely imaginary, resulting in a corresponding Noether charge that indicates the disorder of corresponding gauge theory.  We show that the algebra formed by surface charge flux conservation laws is equivalent to the Virasoro algebra.

Accurate analysis of DNA sequences relies on effective detection of patterns
linking genetic disorders. Current methods, though successful in highlighting
recurring DNA patterns, fail to capture unique, rare patterns that may be
discrete or overlapping. To address this, our research introduces the first
large-scale, unattended learning method capable of analyzing individual DNA
component sequences. Our model relies on a comprehensive, combined analysis
of single DNA base sequences and combined bases, unlocking insights into
rational understanding of DNA patterns. We showcase our approach's efficacy
using extensive simulations of two distinct models: a simple model with overlapping
patterns and a complex model replicating the structure of methylated CpG sites.

The existence of a metal-insulator transition in thin V$_2$O$_3$ films prepared by molecular beam epitaxy was investigated. Both V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films with a flat surface and those with roughness exceeding 13 Angstroms showed behavior consistent with bulk materials, exhibiting a transition at 160 K that changed from 6 mOhm/cm when in contact to 12 kOhm/cm when isolated. However, films with surface roughness not exceeding 3.5 Angstroms did not exhibit this transition, instead remaining in an insulating state at 2K and showing resistance an order of magnitude higher than that of the surface termination. The data indicate that the metal-insulator transition's energy scale is severely affected by the introduction of defects at the surface, further suggesting that the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ is driven by the correlation between electrons near the surface.

We investigate a Lie-Poisson system on the $2n$-dimensional Lie algebra of smooth vector fields on a 2-dimensional manifold, showing that smooth, symplectic properties are inherent in the Lie-Poisson system if it's clebschizable. Moreover, a necessary and sufficient condition is found for such a system to be generalized Hamiltonian. By applying this result, we clarify the smooth Hamiltonian form of the generalized Lie-Poisson formula for smooth coadjoint orbits and demonstrate that a smooth representation of $SE(2,1)$ can be turned into a generalized Hamiltonian vector field.

The team has completed a comprehensive analysis of microlensing planets identified by the KMTNet mission, which has significantly expanded our knowledge of gravitational lensing. A particular achievement is the discovery of five new planets found in 2018, bringing the total to nine in the non-prime field, which greatly enhances our understanding of planetary demographics. Out of these nine discovered planets, five have significant "tilts" in their orbital alignment, which could be influenced by the planet's presence affecting its parent star's resonance explanation for the "tilt". A plot showcasing the distribution of planets found through non-prime field detections, which displays a clear divide between random and systematic patterns as per past discoveries, reveals an established trend. Moreover, four out of five "tilted" planets display an established trend of having close orbital relationships. Statistical analysis using a null-hypothesis testing framework confirms the significance of this finding, which has far-reaching implications - given this phenomenon correlates with planet proximity to its parent star, a comparable proportion of near-star planets is expected to exhibit similar behavior. A comprehensive examination of planetary tilts using all available prime and non-prime datasets confirms this phenomenon, establishing a distinct group apart from planets exhibiting little or no orbital distortion. A substantial number of tilting planets exists within close orbital relationships, which demonstrates a distinct group with a different gravitational influence pattern.

Achieving a precise mathematical representation of essential physical properties like conservation of mass and momentum in fluid dynamics requires a delicate balance between accuracy and computational stability, especially when dealing with irregular domains that necessitate a non-uniform spatial grid. A novel strategy has been developed, involving the simultaneous finite-element approximation of both the conserved quantities and their associated fluxes. This method is flexible as it can maintain a consistent discretization error while handling complex boundaries and non-standard grid structures with ease. A key benefit of this approach lies in its ability to exploit a consistent set of assumptions uniformly across the domain without compromising its accuracy, a significant advantage over traditional methods. Furthermore, this technique extends beyond the scope of irregular domains, offering valuable insights and enhancements even in ideal scenarios. In this study, our proposed method has been applied to the Navier-Stokes equations, allowing for consistent results in both steady-state and dynamic simulations. A key outcome of this research is that a stable and accurate numerical solution can be obtained without prior knowledge of the solution itself, a significant aspect that addresses long-standing challenges in Navier-Stokes simulations.

This paper evaluates 20 machine learning methods for three classes based on the NASA's Near Earth Object dataset, which contains datasets for near Earth objects, asteroids, and comets. It is then cross-validated using the k-fold method to assess classification and regression capabilities. Cometti's algorithm is proposed as a feature selection metric, which is applied to each class. Following this, a dataset reduction is performed using multivariate analysis to simplify the features, followed by an evaluation of the most significant attributes using correlation analysis and sequential feature selection. Consequently, the top-performing models for each class are identified, which demonstrate robustness across the three classes.

We define the q-chromatic symmetric polynomial as a q-analog of the chromatic symmetric polynomial.  Our contribution is to derive an expression for this q-analog in terms of multi-parameter q-homogeneous generators associated with Edmonds' polynomial.  By employing 'q-rook theory', we provide an alternative expression for the q-chromatic symmetric polynomial, thereby offering a possible approach for a broader generalization of the chromatic polynomial to multivariate associations.  In addition, our results for a specific q and large q show a striking similarity with a mathematical concept known as 'gluing of walks', a topic studied by Don Zagier.  In order to present these results, we necessity to utilize the language of partitions and the language of walks, providing a clear connection between the two.  Our analysis specifically examines Dyck paths and the associated q-chromatic symmetric polynomials, enabling us to derive comprehensive information about the coefficients involved when expanding q-chromatic symmetric polynomials into power series.

Deep learning models, particularly convolutive networks, have proven to overcome challenging issues of oriented texture classification. One critical factor contributing to this capability is the ability to break down complex orientation-dependent patterns into basic feature components, weighted and merged across the grid. Notably, current models fail to explore orientation capabilities or clearly demonstrate their orientation-based design principles, sparking our investigation into this phenomenon. We hypothesize that only top-level fully convolutional networks possess orientation capabilities due to incorporating orientation-dependent components, and lower-level networks do not exhibit such properties. To verify this assumption, we developed a weighted image classification model utilizing an orientation convolutive module, expected to isolate base features from their grid-dependent combinations. Our experiment results show that the proposed model successfully reduces the dependence on high-level fully convolutional layers, allowing low-level networks to capture oriented patterns as well. Crucially, this finding sheds light on the underlying mechanism of top-level orientation convolutive networks and lays the groundwork for future research on low-level orientation capabilities in deep networks.

Building on the concept of linear intervals from [Gr-SSC], we broaden the scope to include curved linear intervals, characterized by $G$-invariant distributions that can be factored into the localization of tempered global measures on curved test functions derived from compactly supported model sets on $X\backslash B$, where $X$ is a compact locally compact second countable space and $B$ a Borel subset. Next, we establish a new relative trace formula that links the dynamic count of the curved linear intervals to the orbital integrals of the dual group $\hat{G}$. Finally, we demonstrate the trace formula's applicability to various geometric contexts, including the finite trace formula for curved linear intervals on the Borel spectrum of automorphic cusp forms, the Chowla's conjecture, and the Sato-Gindikin conjecture.

The measurement of the top quark mass in the 7 TeV proton-proton collisions at the LHC is reported. Using the inclusive top quark cross section data provided by the ATLAS detector and the next-to-next-to-leading-order perturbative QCD calculations within the fixed-order framework of NNLOPS, the top quark mass is determined by varying its substantial flavor dependence, considering all relevant flavor schemes. By cross-referencing with theoretical calculations of the top quark mass in the on-shell scheme, the impact of the substantial flavor dependence on the top quark mass is assessed. Furthermore, a comparison with the World Average top quark mass value as of March 2021 is made.

A graph is considered nearly regular if the difference between its highest and lowest valence is minimal. In a graph with $n$ vertices and density $\varepsilon$, defining a pair of adjacent vertices requires at least two distinct colors. In 2014, researchers established that on specific types of nearly regular graphs, and in a particular arrangement, at least $\varepsilon n$ colors were needed over multiple stages. Since then, researchers have improved this finding several times. This research was conducted by multiple authors including Chia, Yufei, Liu, Ming, and Wang. In our research, we have improved the previous results to apply not only to graphs with inter-node connections, but also to graphs with inter-edge connections, and we have expanded the scope to include a broader set of nearly regular graphs with higher degree of symmetry, using powerful mathematical tools from Galois theory combined with logical and computational methods that provide color patterns in a structured, cyclic manner.

We have derived a hypercontractive inequality for functions within the weighted Berman space associated with $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a measure with a specific properties. This hypercontractive inequality provides a sharp alternative to the fourteenth Majorization inequality introduced by Carlen and SaffarYazdi. Furthermore, as a significant extension, we established the hypercontractivity of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator in the context of the weighted Berman space.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an increased demand for accurate and rapid diagnosis of chest CT scans. Despite the issue of contamination during data collection, datasets can be expanded through the use of augmented imagery. This study proposes an improved diagnosis method, known as the HT-CD2LDC, that utilizes augmented, three-dimensional, radiological expertise-oriented data. It employs a network called TwCapNet, an advanced, time-distributed capsule network that achieves high diagnostic accuracy and requires minimal learning from a specialist. The network consists of an initial layer that extracts detail-rich, 3D sensory input and two subsequent layers that contribute to depth and context. The results show that HT-CD2LDC performs superiorly to other leading methods, with an overall accuracy of 98.64% in detecting COVID-19 from augmented, augmented, and mixed datasets. Furthermore, HT-CD2LDC was found to be resilient to augmented, augmented, and mixed data privacy breaches. The study used various experimental scenarios simulating varying numbers of patients and COVID-19 cases.
